full_judgment:
ABM Khairul Haque J : This Rule arises out of the judgment and decree dated 4-6-2005, passed by the District Judge, Dhaka, in Civil Revision No. 26 of 2005, in setting aside the judgment and order dated 15-1-2005, passed by the Joint District Judge, Arbitration Court, Dhaka, in Review Miscellaneous Case No. 18 of 2004, rejecting the application for review. 

 3. After a contested hearing the learned Judge by his judgment and decree dated 12-10-2004 dismissed the suit. Being aggrieved the plaintiff filed a review application under Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, being Review Miscellaneous Case No. 18 of 2004. After hearing the said review, miscellaneous case was also dismissed by the order dated 15-1-2005 Being aggrieved by the said order passed by the learned Joint District Judge, the plaintiff obtained a Rule in the Court of District Judge, under section 115(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure. After hearing he Rule, the learned District Judge, by his Judgment and decree dated 4-6-2005 in allowing the revisional application, set aside the order dated 15-1-2005, passed in Review Miscellaneous Case No. 18 of 2004 and also set-aside the Judgment and decree dated 12-10-2004, passed by the trial Court and decreed the suit. Accordingly, a decree in the said Civil Revision was drawn under Order XLI, rule 35 of the Code. Being aggrieved, the defendant obtained the present Rule under section 115(4) of the Code. 

 6. Mr Md Muzibur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submitted that in the facts and circumstances of this case, the judgment and decree passed by the learned District Judge, is misconceived as he dealt with the issues as a first appeal in ignoring the specific provisions of Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code. He further submitted that since there is no error apparent on the face of the record in the impugned judgment and decree passed in the trial Court in Title Suit No. 3 of 2004, the learned District Judge, Dhaka, erred in law, apparent on the face of the record and, as such, the said judgment and decree are to be set aside. 

 7. On the other hand, Mr A Zalil Gazi, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-opposite party, submitted that the learned Joint District Judge erred in law in disposing of the review miscellaneous case as his order was not a speaking order and the learned Judge failed to appreciate the errors apparent on the face of the record as envisaged in Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code, as such, the learned District Judge, under section 115(2) of the Code rightly set aside the said order passed by the learned Joint District Judge. 

 8. We have heard the learned Advocates of both the sides, perused the provisional application, counter-affidavit, etc. We have gone through the judgment and order dated 12-10-2004 passed in Title Suit No. 3 of 2004 and the order dated 15-1-2005 passed in the Review Miscellaneous Case No. 18 of 2004, passed by the Joint District Judge. 

 9. It is true that the Order of the learned Joint District Judge in disposing of the review miscellaneous case, is a short one but at the same time the judgment and decree passed by the learned District Judge in disposing of the revisional application in respect of the legality of the said order passed in review, appears to be a judgment in appeal from the decree in the suit and not on a review miscellaneous case. The principle of review has been spelt out in rule 1 under Order XLVII of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 11. In the instant case admittedly no new document was sought to be produced on behalf of the plaintiff-opposite party. The question of some substantive cause was also not argued. But it was argued that the petition for review raised various errors which are apparent on the face of the record and those are sufficient reasons for allowing the petition and, as such, the learned District Judge rightly decreed the suit. 

 12. Let us first understand what is an error apparent on the face of the record. This has been explained in the case of AHM Mustain Billah vs Bangladesh 2005 BCR (AD) I = 57 DLR (AD) 41. The concept of error apparent on the face of the record has been explained by Md Fazlul Karim, J at paragraphs 27-28 at p. 11 : 

 28. Though there is no hard and fast rule as to what is an error apparent on the face of the record but the same depends on the facts and circumstances of each case. But there could not be an error apparent on the face of the record merely because two possible views as to the interpretation or application of law vis-a-vis the particular facts of a case, one view accepted by the Court though may be erroneous but could not be the ground of review even if a decision or order is erroneous in law or on merits, the same shall not amount to an eror apparent on the face of the record. 

 15. The scope of review, as we have already pointed out earlier above, is very narrow and the learned Judge is not allowed to re-open the case all over again in considering a petition for review. In considering such a petition, a Judge needs to identify the errors and other sufficient reasons, if any.
